question: How does `dotnet ef migrations add` decide what changed?
options: It diffs the C# model against the committed model snapshot
It connects to the database and diffs the live schema against the model
It reads a declarative schema file in the solution and converts its differences into C#
It records the SQL you ran manually in a database console since the last migration
explanation: EF Core diffs model against snapshot at development time and writes the operations as a C# migration you review and commit. It never inspects the live database; assuming it does leads people to skip reviewing the generated file.

question: You rename `Product.Name` to `Product.Title` and the generated migration contains `DropColumn("Name")` and `AddColumn("Title")`. What do you do?
options: Apply it as generated; EF Core copies the data from the dropped column into the added one
Delete the model snapshot file and run `migrations add` again so EF Core detects the rename
Switch to `EnsureCreated()` for this change, because it handles renames without migrations
Edit `Up` and `Down` to use `RenameColumn`, then review and apply
explanation: A drop plus an add deletes every value in the column. Microsoft warns that a migration may drop a column when the intent was to rename it, and the migration is code you are expected to edit. EF Core does not copy data, and `EnsureCreated()` bypasses migrations entirely.

question: Your company's DBA must read and approve every SQL statement before it runs in production. Which strategy fits?
options: Build a migration bundle in CI, which prints its SQL for review before it runs
Generate an idempotent SQL script with `dotnet ef migrations script`
Run `dotnet ef database update` on the production server after a code review
Call `MigrateAsync()` at application startup with SQL logging switched on
explanation: Scripts are the strategy for review-gated deployments: `--idempotent --output migrations.sql` produces a file the DBA can read, and the idempotent form applies only missing migrations. A bundle is the choice for automated deployment, but it does not currently let you inspect the SQL it will execute, so it does not satisfy a review gate.

question: An API runs as five container replicas and each one calls `MigrateAsync()` in its entrypoint. What does Microsoft recommend instead?
options: Keep it; EF Core 9+ takes a lock, so migrating from every replica is the preferred production setup
Install the SDK in the image and run `dotnet ef database update` from each replica's entrypoint
Run a migration bundle once as a deployment job
Call `EnsureCreated()` instead, which is safe to run from several replicas in parallel
explanation: The applying-migrations page says not to make every replica run migrations from its entrypoint and not to install the SDK in the app image; generate a bundle in CI and run it once with an identity that has schema permissions. The lock in EF Core 9+ prevents corruption, but runtime migration still needs elevated permissions and gives no review or coordinated rollout.

question: A pull request changes the model but the author forgot to add a migration. How can CI catch it before deployment?
options: It cannot; the error only appears when users hit the new column in production
Run `dotnet ef migrations list`, which exits with an error when the model changed
Compile the project; the C# compiler reports a model that has no matching migration
Run `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes` in the pipeline
explanation: `has-pending-model-changes` (EF Core 8+) checks the model against the last migration. `migrations list` only lists migrations and their state. Since EF Core 9, `Migrate` also throws on pending model changes, but that is at deploy time, later than CI.

question: A migration has already been applied to staging and production, and you spot a wrong column length in it. What is the correct fix?
options: Fix the model and add a new migration that alters the column
Edit the applied migration file with the right length and redeploy
Delete its row from `__EFMigrationsHistory` so that the fixed migration runs again
Run `dotnet ef migrations remove`, fix the model, and add the migration again
explanation: Environments that already ran a migration will never run it again, so editing it creates drift between databases. `migrations remove` is for the last migration that has not been applied yet. A new migration keeps every environment on the same path.
